scopeReview: PSO-2.D.1–2: political/economic/social and environmental consequences of population distribution/density, service provision and carrying capacity. Hypothetical political rules and resource figures are not legal or medical advice; human choices and environmental constraints both retained.
varietyReview: Four interpreted stimuli address service access, per-person energy, political representation and total demand; seven applications cover capacity assumptions, shared networks, dispersed delivery, habitat, drought, housing and resource-source scales. Varied keys/difficulty and all five skills represented.
repetitionReview: Different from2.1: interprets consequences rather than repeating definitions of three densities. Aquifer balance from1.5 is not reissued with new numbers; demand comparison changes both population and consumption, while drought uses a distinct conditional ratio argument.

questions.correctOption: The dispersed area’s longer mean journey shows why equal service ratios need not mean equal geographic access.
questions.independentReview: Independently computed both ratios10000/1=10000 residents/clinic, then compared35>5 minutes. The inference concerns geographic journeys, not an unmeasured clinical-quality difference.

questions.correctOption: Higher density is associated here with lower transport energy per resident, but other impacts and causes are not established.
questions.independentReview: Checked per-capita sequence12000,8000,4000 and distinguished it from totals with unknown denominators. No claim of zero environmental burden or a density-only intervention effect is supported.

questions.correctOption: Each southern representative serves four times as many residents as each northern representative.
questions.independentReview: Recomputed each population/representative ratio with denominator1 and southern/northern ratio4000/1000=4. No legal entitlement or actual electoral judgment is inferred.

questions.correctOption: Both areas demand 100,000 units per year, despite their different populations and densities.
questions.independentReview: Independently multiplied1000*100=100000 and10000*10=100000, with densities1000/100=10 and10000/100=100. Distinct population and consumption effects offset; units are annual demand, not stocks.

questions.correctOption: The estimate depends partly on the assumed resource use and means of obtaining and managing resources.
questions.independentReview: Compared two models of the same resource base with different demand or technology parameters. Their outputs can differ conditionally; this does not establish unlimited capacity or validate current use by its existence.

questions.correctOption: Shared infrastructure may reduce some per-resident costs, while capacity limits can still create problems.
questions.independentReview: Distinguished a potential shared-network efficiency from guarantees of universal benefit. The prompt supplies coordinated networks but not costs, prices or resident incomes.

questions.correctOption: The trade-off between reaching dispersed residents and the cost of covering long service routes
questions.independentReview: Matched the intervention to dispersed origins and route coverage. No medical treatment recommendation or asserted outcome is made; this is a spatial service-delivery comparison.

questions.correctOption: Concentrated demand can increase land-use pressure, while planning and consumption shape the outcome.
questions.independentReview: Distinguished pressure from a guaranteed outcome and local exposure from national averaging. The scenario does not quantify actual habitat removal or mandate a particular policy.

questions.correctOption: It increases relative to the available supply, so a formerly supportable demand may no longer be sustainable.
questions.independentReview: Held demandD>0 fixed and decreased supplyS>0; D/S increases. No numerical shortage date or universal response is inferred from that inequality.

questions.correctOption: Area-wide population density does not specify housing supply, room counts or how residents are distributed among dwellings.
questions.independentReview: Constructed a counterexample with equal residents/land but different numbers of available rooms. This refutes an equality claim about crowding without drawing medical or individual conclusions.

questions.correctOption: The connected source regions as well as the city’s consumption and resource flows
questions.independentReview: Followed imports backward to source regions, distinguishing local support from the wider geography of demand. No invented footprint value or claim that all imports are unsustainable is introduced.
